state.core_question: 로마 콘크리트는 어떻게 작은 균열을 스스로 메우며 이 반응은 오래 버티는 데 어떻게 기여할까?

evidence.facts: Ancient bedding mortar sampled from Privernum city wall, not Colosseum. Modern crack-sealing test used Roman-inspired mortar with Portland cement, fly ash, sand and quicklime; gap 0.5 ±0.1 mm; 28 days submerged curing plus two months wet/dry preconditioning; 30-day water-flow test; negligible flow after 1-3 weeks depending on crack geometry. No building-scale structural recovery test.

Pompeii unfinished construction site evidence supports dry quicklime and pozzolan premixing before water addition. Lime clasts can retain calcium source; dissolution and mineral deposition observed. No new timed crack-flow healing experiment reported.

evidence.source: European Commission JRC, Major concepts EN Eurocodes
evidence.facts: Design working life is the assumed period of intended use with anticipated maintenance, not a material expiration or collapse date.

candidate_claims.C1: Some calcium-rich lime clasts can supply calcium that moves with water and contributes to crack-filling mineral reactions. This mechanism may contribute to durability.
candidate_claims.C2: The Colosseum was proven to heal every crack and restore its original structural strength within three weeks.
candidate_claims.C3: Modern concrete buildings always collapse at 100 years, so Roman concrete lasts twenty times longer.
candidate_claims.C4: Formation sequence (mixing and remaining clasts) must be distinguished from later healing sequence (crack, water, calcium movement, mineral filling).
candidate_claims.C5: A diagram should label laboratory results separately from ancient observations and proposed mechanism.
candidate_claims.C6: The modern mortar experiment proves continuous self-healing for 2000 years.
